utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- I have a small problem, and that is that my case manager is not here as yet. I think there's been some delay with transport or what have you. And there's a matter I just needed to check with Mr. Krajisnik prior to the commencement of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it something that should really be done before you even start, or could you make a beginning and then ask for a time-out of five minutes to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise, we have to wait, and it's uncertain when he will arrive. So if there would be any way to start and then I will grant you five minutes for ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If that's the approach that Your Honour wants to adopt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I asked whether that would be possible, and it seems that it's not totally impossible, so therefore ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not totally impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Chamber will know when your case manager arrives and give you -- give you just a couple of minutes at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But, of course, it's rather disruptive at that stage because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Loukas please speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and in two minutes from now on I would have no hesitation to wait, Ms. Loukas, but it could well be half an hour as well and then we have lost half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can't put a time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Davidovic in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And I inform you that once Ms. Loukas has started her cross-examination that there might be a short interruption of a couple of minutes for some consultation between counsel and Mr. Krajisnik, which could not take place due to the absence of the case manager at this very moment. So please be prepared that there might be a short interruption. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Now, Mr. Davidovic, at -- at a certain point -- I just want to go to your statement. Now, Mr. Davidovic, how long have you been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1974. Between 1974 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So that's about 20 years. Now, I want to take you to --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to the statement that you gave the Prosecution. It indicates on the front of the statement that it went from the 14th to the 19th of November and the 25th to the 29th of January. So this procedure of -- of taking your statement in consultation with Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution, that took a process of -- in the nature of 11 days; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't recall exactly to the day, but roughly speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just point out: In the second half of last year, I was also involved in information talks about the circumstances, et cetera, and then afterwards The Hague Tribunal asked the Federal Government to release me from the need to keep state secrets. And then afterwards we could go ahead. Because I did not want to get involved in any talks if I did not have that waiver from the Federal Government.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Davidovic, I was specifically asking you about the time it took to take your statement. But this additional information in relation to -- if you could just point out -- "in the second half of last year, I was also involved in information talks." Who participated in those information talks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first conversation that they attempted to have with me was at Brcko, and the Prosecutor and somebody else were present. And when I referred to the fact that I would need to get that waiver in terms of official and state secrets, they said that they would request that. And it took rather a long time until they final got it. And then afterwards the Prosecutor invited me for another talk, and there was the Prosecutor himself and an investigator, I think, from the Tribunal. I think he was a police officer by profession. And there was an interpreter there. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So who was involved in these information talks? Who was present when you were having these information talks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, other than myself and these three people I've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And who were these three people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat it once again. The Prosecutor, then somebody else - I believe it was a policeman; I don't know his name, also on behalf of The Hague Tribunal - and a lady, who was an interpreter. No one else. And those three people were always present there throughout, and nobody else participated in the talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, perhaps it's helpful to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's help to feel find out whether the information talks are anything different from the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. That's what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. If we could ask the witness to take off his headphones for a moment, I might be able to address the Court and Ms. Loukas and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's then first try to find out whether the witness understands any English. Mr. Davidovic, do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you, then, please take off your earphones for a second. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can advise Ms. Loukas and the Court that I -- that I was present, I think, at what he's talking about as informational talks. I was present with an investigator from the OTP named Paul Basham. Another investigator, Peter Mitford-Burgess, and an interpreter. I don't remember who the interpreter was on that occasion. When we first met him, we were in Brcko talking to other people. His name had come up as someone who might have information for us. We met briefly with him, maybe 15 minutes or so, just to determine if he was the Mico Davidovic whose name had come up in the course of our investigation. He indicated to us that he would be willing to talk with us, but he wouldn't do so until he had a waiver from his government to talk about matters that had occurred when he had been employed as a police officer. And there was no statement taken and no information written about -- there might have been a mission report that just mentioned the fact that we met with him, but there wasn't any substantive conversation with him, other than we would seek a waiver and we would try to talk to him in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I then understand that on the 14th of November the real interview started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I hope this will assist you. And we could ask the witness to put his earphones on again, I take it, or would you like to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd just be interested in having perhaps any documentation that the Prosecution have in relation to the information talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honour, there was no substance recorded of the meeting with him other than the fact that we had met with and that we were going to seek a waiver. I'll try and find whatever sentence there might be in the mission report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, then I take it that you will receive that; although, it might not be much. Mr. Davidovic, could you please put your earphones on again. Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: How long did these information talks take?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean every day or how many days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, let me just -- let me just -- it takes too much time. When you for the first time met with anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor, how much time did that first meeting take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very brief. Perhaps half an hour, 40 minutes tops. It was a very brief meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it at that occasion that you insisted on getting a waiver before you would further talk to representatives of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And what sort of waiver did you get?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a document from the Federal Government, from the Committee for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and it indicated that I was given a waiver in -- as far as state, military, and official secrets were concerned, and that meant that I could freely answer any questions put to me by The Hague investigators without bearing any individual responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in any event, going back to the statement that you ultimately gave to the Prosecution, it was of course a very detailed statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the -- and as a police officer of some 20 years standing, you were very keenly aware of the need to be truthful and correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor asked you to tell them anything you knew about Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't ask me to talk about Mr. Krajisnik. He asked me to tell him what I did, where I was, and what I saw when I spent time on the territory of the Republika Srpska in the first place and then within a larger, broader context what I did within the area of competence for the federal secretariat, federal SUP. I was not even told that their main interest was Mr. Krajisnik. They asked me to tell them what I did and where I went and where I met with a number of people. Initially I didn't even know that the whole point was to investigate Mr. Krajisnik. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, you were aware that these proceedings were ongoing, I take it, proceedings against Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that proceedings were underway against Mr. Milosevic and against a number of other people, so I thought it was about that. And initially -- even for the first few days I had no idea that it was mostly about Mr. Krajisnik, because there are quite a few trials and proceedings underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I want to take you to paragraph 61 of your statement that you've given the Prosecution. And you indicated there that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, would you like the witness to be provided with the statement or not? If not, then ask Mr. Usher to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, there's no real need to it. I'm just adverting to it so that we're all on the same page, as it were, in the courtroom, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would you mind if he has it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I don't mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You indicated there that you filed certain reports and that you kept copies of these reports. And then you indicate that they were taken possession of by the Serbian MUP personnel during a search of your private residence in Belgrade in 1995. Now, just in relation to that, you'll recall that the Prosecutor asked you some questions about that. And firstly that was at page 78 of the transcript on the 9th of June, Your Honours. And then Judge Hanoteau also asked you some questions, at page 81. Now, just in relation to that, tell me, you indicated to Judge Hanoteau that they issued you a certificate which showed that they'd taken items that were of interest. Now, did you have a conversation with the police officers prior to them issuing this certificate to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had not talked to anyone. I wasn't even there when they came in. It is not a certificate as such. It is about a search warrant and a paper indicating what items had been taken, and it stayed with the person who at that particular moment was in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, in response to a question from His Honour Judge Hanoteau, you indicated -- sorry. If I might just check what you just said. Okay. Let's just get the sequence correct here. The police officers introduced themselves and they show you a search warrant; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that misstates the evidence. He's not indicated he was present when the search actually took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's not immediately apparent from the answer that he gave Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps not necessarily. But is it part of the evidence? I mean, even if it would not be in response to a question of Judge Hanoteau, it's still to be ... Mr. Hannis, could you guide us to the page where that appears?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on page 10 he said, "I wasn't even there when they came in." Page 10, line 2 and 3 from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, let's just have a look at what you told Judge Hanoteau. You said: "When they entered the flat, they introduced themselves as MUP officials. They showed their identity cards and the -- and the search that they had. They didn't provide this to me. But when they entered the flat, they tried to find out where my documents were, and that's what the search was interested in. After they had finished the search, they issued a certificate which showed that they had taken items that were of interest to the Davidovic case in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So you tell the Court that that information that you provided in response to a question from Judge Hanoteau was information based on you not being there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are trying to imply something that I did not say, and especially I did not say it in the way that you are trying to interpret it. I was quite clear. When these people came along, I was not present, I was not in the flat, and I was not there when the search was carried out. There was somebody else there, who opened the door and told them who he was, and then they introduced themselves as police officers. They showed the search warrant, et cetera. I told you what they did. But let me stress once again, I was not present in the flat when the search was carried out. I don't know why you keep insisting on that and why you keep implying that I said that I was actually there. I was not there. I never said I was there. And I would not have been in a position to say something like that because it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you're telling the Court that you weren't there, but let's have a look at what you told the Court. Okay. Let's go to page 78 of the 9th of June, shall we? Mr. Hannis asks you this question: "In your statement, you say that you kept copies of these reports but you don't have them any longer. Why is that?" And your answer was: "I did write a report and send it to the minister. It was dispatched to the minister. And I asked for instructions on what to do next, and I gave a detailed account of what was going on and what my view was. That document went to the federal minister, and I had a copy, but that copy afterwards was taken away from me and I never managed to find it again." Okay. That's what you told the Court in answer to a question from the Prosecutor. In answer to a question from Judge Hanoteau - I've already read out what your response was in relation to that - and that is that they issued a certificate and what have you. And when one looks at your statement at paragraph 61, which you have in front of you, nowhere do you indicate that you were not there, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, let's try to find out what the source of knowledge of the witness is when he gave his statement, when he gave his testimony, because he never said he was not there until today. He never said that he was there. So therefore let's try to find out. Mr. Davidovic, the information about how the search went on, how do you -- how did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I returned to my flat in Belgrade, the person who was there gave me an account of what had happened. He told me that the police had been there. He described how they had introduced themselves and how they searched the flat. They even told him not to call me on the phone and to wait until I come back to my apartment to tell me everything. When I said that all these things had been seized, I meant my personal case files, my dossiers, those that I kept with me. Perhaps that is something that caused some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you return to your flat? How much time after the search took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was during a weekend when I was away, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. On Sunday night when I came back, I was told that they had been to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add something to my answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to let you add something to your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the record that was made when the flat was entered, it was obligatory for two witnesses to be present for the search to be valid and legal. That, however, did not happen. There were no witnesses. And when I saw the record, I could see that there were no witnesses. That is a legal requirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, you as a police officer of 20 years standing, when you wrote your report in relation to -- when you wrote your statement, sorry, in relation to what happened to these reports at paragraph 61, you do not indicate there that you were not present and nor did you indicate in the answers that you gave to the Prosecutor and to the Judge in relation to this sequence that you were not there. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, he did not write the statement. And this is argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if the witness would say -- what answer could he give? That is it there? Then, of course, no one would believe him. If he says that it's not in there, it just confirms what he can read. So I would agree with Mr. Hannis that this is -- well, perhaps again the kind of ritual dances we have talked about before and which really do not assist the Chamber very much. Please come to your points. We'd like to hear about them, but this makes not enough sense to spend time on it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will make one comment. The common-law process of closing the gates in cross-examination is no mere ritual dance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. We have -- we have talked about closing the doors and opening windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not a jury.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But nevertheless this is a police officer of 20 years standing. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, you've said that five times. You've asked him how long he was a police officer, although we read in the statement that he was a police officer since 1974. Then you calculated for us that that is 20 years. The Chamber would even be in a position to make that -- make that relatively small calculation. Then you started almost every question with "with your 20 years of police standing." I mean, the Chamber is now aware that every answer comes from a police officer which worked for 20 years in the police services.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the Trial Chamber would expect more of a police officer of 20 years in his statement than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But that's clear. That doesn't need repetition again and again and again. Whatever question you ask to this witness, the Chamber will be aware and will be constantly aware whether this is satisfactory for someone who worked for 20 years in the police services. Please be assured that we really are aware. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to another portion of your statement, shall we? That's paragraph 200. You don't need the statement in front of you for that purpose. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I notice that Mr. Karganovic entered the courtroom. If you would need the time now, then of course we would give you the couple of minutes you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my case manager just wishes to extend his apologies to the Court. But what occurred is that his badge expired this morning so that he could not enter the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bureaucracy sometimes reigns our lives, Ms. Loukas. Of course you're excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, in your statement that -- prior to you coming -- at the beginning of your evidence in chief you indicated to the Prosecution was truthful and accurate. You indicate there that "Karadzic and Krajisnik had a fist-fight in the plane," basically on the way back from New York in, you say, either 1991 or 1992, "over money." You know what I'm talking about, don't you? This thing you put in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, Mr. Krajisnik did not go to New York in 1991 or 1992. Now, are you prepared to concede that that information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not prepared. I was informed by the members of our services who accompanied them, and that's how I know about it. I cannot go into any details. I was just informed by the members of our service when they were both on the plane. I think when they were on a plane to New York or somewhere. It concerned the money collected from our emigres abroad, and I think it was this service in New York. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, that was just passing on gossip, and you as a police officer know better than that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was gossip. It was a note that I was able to see, drafted by two of the officers who accompanied them. I said I couldn't be certain, but I think it concerned New York. It was a long time ago, and I don't know all the places, all the cities they visited. I think it was New York. The first time they went, they said they had no access and then the second time they were able to go after all to this club of emigres, displaced persons, whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you very specifically state in your statement: "At the end of 1991 or the beginning of 1992, Karadzic and Krajisnik went to New York for negotiations at the UN." That's what you put in your statement. You now tell the Court, "I couldn't be certain. I think it concerned New York." You're just making this up as you go along, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are not telling the truth. I am telling you about the information that was available to me, that I had access to, and that I gave to investigators when they asked me, because they put questions to me concerning certain details of my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, Ms. Loukas confronts you with your statement where you said that "Upon returning from New York, that there was a fight," and in your testimony now you say that you're not certain that it was New York. That's what she's confronting you with. Are you not certain that it was New York?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was New York. She's saying that it wasn't. I cannot be certain. I said what I knew. I didn't make anything up. At that moment, I believed it was New York, and I still think it was. Now she's saying they had never been there, and I'm no longer certain. I really can't swear one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It, at least, where your statement seems to be quite positive about it, it seems that being confronted with what Ms. Loukas puts to you, you are not that positive anymore. And Ms. Loukas as a matter of fact is confronting you with the fact that where the statement seems to be clear and unambiguous, that from your testimony now something different appears.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said at the outset, and I asked you to understand that I cannot remember all the details, places, days and hours. Indeed, I made some corrections when I came here concerning some places that are mentioned, like Geneva or Athens. I thought in this particular case it was New York, but maybe I misunderstood at the time. But the essence of what I said, I stand by still today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to make two observations: First of all, Ms. Loukas, you've made your point. Second - and I'm now addressing both parties - I take it that a journey in the end of 1991, early 1992 to negotiate with the UN is something that hardly could have been a total secret. So, Mr. Hannis, I can imagine that you would have -- must have sources to verify whether this is correct, whether this statement in this respect is correct, yes or no. Therefore, it would certainly assist if these matters could be clarified. At the same time, I'm aware, Ms. Loukas, that you're referring to part of the statement which is not tendered into evidence but of which you're perfectly free to ask questions about the statement he gave. Mr. Hannis, is there any way of, well, taking a position on whether this could be correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not done checking to see whether or not there was ever a trip, whether it was 1991, 1992, or perhaps a later date. But as you know, I did not offer this as part of the statement that we proposed in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I can imagine the Defence has a keen interest in not only seeking verification of the parts you have admitted into evidence but also to see whether -- how reliable the other parts are that are taken out perhaps for other reasons but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Along this line, when we get this kind of information, as you know, we often make a request for assistance from the authorities. For example, to see if we could get a copy of the report that would have been provided by the two security officers who in this case he got information from. But our success in getting those kinds of information has generally not been very good, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One is the report. The other is the visit itself, which I think you would not be dependent on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. And I can do some checking on that and we'll advise the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another topic, Mr. Davidovic. Let's go to -- as I indicated, let's go to another topic. You gave evidence on the 10th of June. That's last Friday. And this is at page 9 of the transcript, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. And the question was this, from

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Mr. Davidovic, my question was: Do you know if Arkan was subordinate to anyone?" And you indicated in your answer there that "I think he was subordinated to -- well, partly to the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia, to Mico Stanisic, and I assume that President Krajisnik -- or rather, Mr. Karadzic were aware of his activities." Okay. The first point to make there is that your evidence to -- that you gave in court in response to the question from the Prosecution is -- is quite clearly an assumption on your part; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not an assumption. I can give you some details that might convince you whether I had indeed information that allows me to say what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Davidovic, so when you use the term in response to the question from the Prosecution "and I assume that" - right? - you weren't assuming. You just said you were assuming, but you weren't assuming. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what your interpretation is as to whether I was assuming or not assuming, but I can give you additional information and then you will be able to assess yourself whether it is knowledge or assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'm -- this is not interpretation. I'm quoting your words in court. All right? And your words were "and I assume that President Krajisnik -- or rather, Mr. Karadzic was aware of his activities." Those are your words, not my words. So when you use the word "assume," are you telling this Court that you were wrongly using the word "assume"? Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not misuse this word. I was a witness to that conversation and I was an eyewitness to the relevant incidents, and he was there, so it's impossible that he didn't know. Two things happened: One at the Bosnian villa, and another one that was assisted also by Ratko Mladic and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic -- okay. So "assume" means something different to you, does it? What does "assume" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means I'm familiar with the situation. We are talking about matters where I was present, where people like Frenki were present. You are trying to use this game of words, whether it is the truth or not the truth, whether I know or assume. It's more playing with words on your part.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference, isn't there, between knowing something and assuming something, and you as a police officer of 20 years standing, you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some things need not to be explained because they are known. I assume that certain things are known facts. That is what I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Davidovic. Anyway, that's what you said on page 9 of the 10th of June. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: -- [In English] Or rather Mr. Karadzic was aware of his activities -- [Interpretation] When you said that President Karadzic or Krajisnik were aware of his activities, did you mean to say -- did you mean that Mr. Krajisnik was not aware? Is that what you meant when you said that and that only Mr. Karadzic knew about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "Mr. Krajisnik" and then I said "Mr. Karadzic" as well. Had there been a question like that, a specific question, I would be in a position to say when I found out about it, when I was present, and when I heard these topics being discussed and Arkan and his men being present. When I talked to the Prosecutor, I didn't go into details, nor did they ask me to go into every minute detail as to what I heard where. But since my statement is rather extensive, I had to cover all the places where I'd been. I was not able to go into all the details. And if any clarification is necessary, I'm prepared to give it. And I can go into much greater detail than I did in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead. Could we hear about these details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me - and I didn't say this even to the Prosecution when we went to Lukavica, to the barracks where I came upon the request of my minister, Petar Gracanin, to report to Mr. Ratko Mladic and when Mr. Karadzic came. One officer who opened the door - he was probably from Mladic's entourage - said that some Arkan's men were at the Lukavica barracks. They had arrived by car. I know that Ratko Mladic then asked Karadzic, "Who are these men? What's going on? What are they doing here?" And then Karadzic said, "Yes. We have certain arrangements that Arkan, too, should be involved in Sarajevo and help with the effort we had started." That was the end of the conversation. There were no more questions about it in my presence. They moved on to another subject. That's how I know that he knew that Arkan's men were there, at Lukavica and in Sarajevo. And that is something that I did not write in my statement, nor did the Prosecutor ask me about any details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just going back to where we were in relation to an assumption that you made. Then His Honour the Presiding Judge, Judge Orie, asked you some more questions about this. And -- and he said to you: "I assume -- yes, but I have one additional question in this respect if you're finished with it. Mr. Davidovic, one of your earlier answers was -- and I assume that President Krajisnik -- or rather, Mr. Karadzic were aware of his activities." Now you switch from President Krajisnik to Karadzic and then you said "were aware." You didn't say "was aware" but "were aware." And then you -- then in response to that question, you say: "No, I'm not ruling out either of them; without that knowledge -- without that knowledge on the part of them, it would not be possible. I think -- I think both Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic are fully aware of that." And then Judge Orie asks you another question. And he says -- and he asks you about whether you have any specific evidence rather than this statement it could not happen without them knowing about it. Then you answer that question by saying that you don't have a single word of praise for Mr. Krajisnik. And let's come to that point. You're actually biassed against Mr. Krajisnik, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not biassed, nor do I see why I would be. I'm just trying to clarify certain matters. You've just asked me a lot of questions. If we go one by one, I can answer each and every one of them. But please don't go on for that long and then end with "isn't it" or "aren't you," because you are just looking for me to say what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you, as a police officer, more than anybody know that this Court is trying to get to the truth and that neither you nor I are going to make the ultimate judgement. You know that, don't you? And you know that the Court, to be fully informed, has got to hear both sides of the story. You know that, don't you? So you do understand --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's not a correct position to take. You understand that, don't you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? I'm telling you what I know, and I'm answering your questions. And as to what is correct and what is not correct, it is not up to me to say; it is up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Davidovic, His Honour the Judge last Friday asks you if you have any information which positively identifies Mr. Krajisnik as being aware of these events. All right? And your response is: "I must the admit I've been asked this before, what can be said about Mr. Krajisnik." And you go on to say, "I have not a single word of praise I can say about Mr. Krajisnik." So when the Judge asks you very specifically about any information that you have, rather than assumption, you answer with, "I have not a single word of praise I can say about Mr. Krajisnik." I'm bound to put this to you and you're bound to disagree.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the interpreters are missing you and -- but since you're not wearing your earphones, you don't receive their messages.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that the -- well, it certainly made it to the transcript, unless I need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Ms. Loukas, the interpreters say, "We can't hear you. Microphone, please." But since you are not wearing your earphones, you don't get these messages from the interpreters, and then you do not speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the interpretation dropped off before she got to her question. Her question does not appear in the transcript. But her question is one that she's already asked and that he already answered, which was: Are you biassed? And he previously answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Well,--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, actually the answer to that question -- well, I'm going to leave that topic alone. It's -- I've got more information to get on with.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Davidovic, that's how you answered that question. His Honour asked you for very specific information, and all you can say is that you don't have a word of praise about Mr. Krajisnik. That's not good enough for a police officer of 20 years, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection. That's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if we look at the transcript of the 10th of June, you may have noticed that I clearly indicated to the witness that he was not invited to give such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was clear to him. And then we went further on whether -- whether he had any specific sources. And we -- I think we ended up in the Bosanska Vila or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, that's -- that's just a summary of what happened in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yep. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to page 14. All right? So finally -- His Honour is still asking you questions. He says, "Please be more specific. You said you were sitting with people, waiting for talks on the same topic and you're sitting with what people? You told us Frenki and Arkan. Were you sitting with them?" And you said: "I was at Bosanska Vila with Mico Stanisic, Pero Mihajlovic and Frenki and Arkan was there as well, and so I was present in the course of the talks and it was in the beginning of in 1992." And you also indicated at page 14 that Mr. Krajisnik was on the premises of Bosanska Vila. And you gave some further evidence in relation to that. And then Mr. Hannis, after that series of questions, says: "This meeting you were talking about, do you know approximately when it was?" And your answer was: "In the beginning of 1992. It could have been April or May, at Bosanska Vila." All right? Now, Mr. Davidovic, you over 11 days produced a very detailed statement. Do you want to tell me where in your statement that piece of information is, or does the Prosecution want to concede that it does not appear in his statement, to shorten proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire specifically -- are we talking about a meeting in Bosanska Vila with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That does not appear in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you, then, may move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you give evidence that Mr. Krajisnik is at Bosanska Vila with Arkan. This is what you tell this Court last Friday. That's just simply not the truth, Mr. Davidovic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it wouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, you've heard the Prosecution concede that it's not in your statement that took -- your very detailed statement that took 11 days to put together. You simply did not tell the Prosecution about this very significant event; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it is supposed to be so significant. I answered to questions put to me. There's a whole range of issues in which I did not provide details or did not answer questions that were not put to me by the investigator. And even what I did say sometimes was too much. But I simply answered the questions that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you are deliberately -- you gave deliberately false evidence about Mr. Krajisnik being in a meeting with Arkan at Bosanska Vila.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this statement, that I gave a full statement, is something that is inadmissible. And the way you are putting it to me is less than fair. I really don't like being treated like this, and I don't like you to talk to me like this. I think there's no reason for that whatsoever. I'm simply telling you what I did and where I was, and don't push me to saying something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, Ms. Loukas is entitled to put to you that she doesn't believe you, that she thinks that you're not speaking the truth, and she may ask those questions. Ms. Loukas, you've done so two or three times. You received the answers. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask for Ms. Loukas not to insult me and not to tell me that I'm telling lies. These are serious words, and I don't like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Davidovic, Ms. Loukas is entitled to ask these questions. She will have her own reasons why she doesn't believe you. Finally it is the Chamber who will make the determination of what the truth is. That is part of the type of proceedings that there are in this Tribunal. It's a way of saying "I don't believe you. Would it not be different from what you said." That's a specific form in which this is put to you. Don't feel insulted, but just concentrate on whether you're certain about your answers you've given before or whether there's any doubt or whether they may be wrong. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour I'm just wondering if we can take an early break at this point. There's just a further matter I need to confirm with my case manager and Mr. Krajisnik at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can have an early break. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed. Oh, we have no witness yet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no witness, Your Honour. I'm happy to make it a one-woman show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I have to deny you that pleasure. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, I just wanted to take you back to some evidence you gave on the 9th of June. That is at page 95, for the Court. And again, His Honour the Presiding Judge, His Honour Judge Orie, was asking you some questions. And he said this: "So the basis of that knowledge is what Vojkan Djurkovic told you, and you said, 'He used to say publicly that he was taking the money to Pale to Karadzic and Krajisnik.' And then you said: 'And he did it in person.' Is that what he told you, or is that what you observed yourself?" And you answer was: "He told me himself, and I heard it on a number of occasions when other people were talking ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please read slower, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I take on board the -- the directive from the interpreters to read a little slower. And that is -- did the interpreters get the last bit or should I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please repeat it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd look at the transcript, you'll see where it stops. Perhaps you'd take the whole quote again, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So His Honour asked you this question: "So the basis of that knowledge is what Vojkan Djurkovic told you, and you said, 'He used to say publicly that he was taking the money to Pale to Karadzic and Krajisnik.' And then you said: 'And he did it in person.' Is that what he told you, or is that what you observed yourself?" And your response was: "He told me himself, and I heard it on a number of occasions when other people were talking about it." And His Honour asked you: "These other people, could you mention their names?" And you gave some names. "For example, a man who is in Bijeljina, Dusko Marjanovic, he's a lawyer there today. Then Gavrilovic, someone who was in charge of a unit during the war. The people from MUP, who were also involved and who witnessed that. And there were some officers there as well." Now, just in relation to that particular aspect, our investigators, Mr. Davidovic, since you gave that evidence have had the opportunity to speak with Mr. Gavrilovic, and he in fact denies that that was said in his presence. Does that in any way -- and I'm offering you this opportunity now. I'm offering you an opportunity to reconsider your evidence in that regard, that Mr. Gavrilovic was present when this statement was made by Mr. Djurkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to object to this form of question at this point. I'm not even sure that we're talking about the same Mr. Gavrilovic. I don't know the circumstances under which he was asked this question. I don't think it's very helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, ultimately, of course, in the Defence case Your Honours will be hearing from the gentleman in question, and I'm offering the witness the opportunity to reconsider his evidence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. I think it's fair that it's put to this witness that the Defence has spoken to a person by the name of Gavrilovic who denies that he was present when this was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My point is, Your Honour, in his evidence this witness just referred to the name of Gavrilovic as somebody who commanded a unit in the war. I don't know what Gavrilovic they're talking about, whether he commanded a unit and whether it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Either you further clarify that. Or the worst that could happen, Mr. Hannis, is that it is another Mr. Gavrilovic and then, of course, we would find out at a later stage that there was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Gavrilovic's first name? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Blago. I know his family name is Gavrilovic. I think it's Blago. But he did not only tell me about that but he gave me a whole range of other essential details. And if you'll allow me, I'll tell you. It was precisely in my conversation with him that I found out about the way in which Muslims were being taken to his area of responsibility and where his battalion was. He was present when events took place, when these people were taken there from Bijeljina and how they were standing there in this no man's land. And of course I'm not denying this. I can state once again that he did say that and I can give you names of a couple of more people who were adamant that this was the way things were done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, first I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that at this moment the subject of the question is not what Mr. Gavrilovic told you but whether Mr. Gavrilovic was present at certain events. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, as I indicated to you previously, our investigators since you gave that evidence have had the opportunity to speak to Mr. Gavrilovic. In fact, a Mr. Blagoje Gavrilovic. And I offered you the opportunity to reconsider your evidence in light of that. Do you reconsider your evidence in light of that, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for that. I can reiterate my statement from before. I am still claiming that he was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this other person that you mentioned, Mr. Dusko Marjanovic, now, he's a friend of yours, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Is Dusko Marjanovic a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have many friends, many people I know, and Dusko is one of them. I've known him for a long time, since childhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's all the question was: He's a friend of yours. So he's a friend of yours, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusko Marjanovic is a security officer for Gavrilovic's unit. If you are asking a question with regard to their relationship, he was the security officer and Gavrilovic was the commander of the unit. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no question about the relationship between Mr. Gavrilovic and this Mr. Marjanovic. The question is simply whether Mr. Marjanovic is a friend of yours. And perhaps, because it seemed that you are struggling a bit with it, you could specify in your answer close friend, friend, acquaintance, someone you happen to know. That's the whole range of -- please try to answer the question as good as you can what your relationship with Mr. Marjanovic in these terms was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was trying to say. It's a bit difficult to describe it properly. Is it a close friend, somebody I'm seeing on a daily basis, or somebody I see only occasionally? What I was trying to say is that I've known him since childhood. We used to be friends as children, and we do know one another now, because I do see him almost every day, but we're not close friends in terms of spending time together every day. We encounter each other, but we are not that close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, on to another topic. Your evidence on the 10th of June on page 34, you indicated in response to a question from the Prosecution: "As far as I know, representatives from the -- a representative from the republican party parliament, Micic, told me that they had discussed the matter at the republican parliament and they wanted an example to be set with regard to confronting these paramilitary formations. However, they nevertheless decided that I should be prevented from taking further action and a request was made for me to withdraw." Now, just in relation to your evidence on that topic, which Mr. Micic are you talking about there? What's the first name of the man you're talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Micic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, that was, of course, a reference to something that's also contained in your statement. And this is in relation to the 20th Session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska held on the 14th and 15th of September, 1992 in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you please guide us by numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I might have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be 158? Is it there where we are?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I think Your Honour is correct. Unfortunately the Post-It with which I'd marked it disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll find our way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in any event, it's a reference to something that's contained within your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not actually the specific paragraph I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's where the name is mentioned but it's not the correct paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our legal officer says that 99 makes a better chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm much obliged to your legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So in paragraph 99 of your statement you indicate that you remained in Bijeljina for a while longer and the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly then passed a resolution which demanded that I be expelled from Bijeljina." Now, just in relation to your evidence on that topic -- yes, and you gave that answer that I've read out to you at page 34 of the transcript. Now, Mr. Davidovic, you were in fact not mentioned at the 20th Assembly Session. And I'm happy to show you a copy of the notes from that session, and that is the stenographic note, not just the minutes, in your language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's something that we don't have. We would like to have a copy of that, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, neither do we have. And apart from that, the -- you're saying the 20th Session. Was that only one in that month, or is there any other? I might have overlooked something.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, there's only that one session. The previous session, Your Honour, was in August and the subsequent session was in October. There was only one session in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't check that at this moment. Well, Mr. Hannis says that he hasn't got this material. Ms. Loukas, how are we going to proceed with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I understand that, Your Honour. I have the 20th Session. I'm happy to place it before the witness so he can see if he can find a reference to himself. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're not going to ask him to go through the stenographic notes for the whole of the -- now right away, isn't it? Otherwise we could take a break for another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm happy for this to be -- I will be tendering this as an exhibit and the Prosecution can make their own translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm happy to look at it and if it doesn't appear in there, I'm happy to stipulate to that. The point is this witness has not testified that he was at the session and heard it said. He testified that he was told that by Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That certainly is the -- I think, Ms. Loukas, we do not disagree that there's no claim of this witness, at least not in this statement that he was present. But he says allegedly and -- so therefore would it not be wiser -- I mean, apart from asking the witness now to -- to go through a lengthy document -- to see whether perhaps later today the Prosecution and Defence could sit together and see whether there's any reference to it. I mean, Mr. Hannis, you might have someone available who speaks and reads some B/C/S and -- go through it and see whether at all the subject, whether or not with the name or without name, is mentioned there before we ask anyone to -- to have it all translated. Especially, Ms. Loukas, if the parties agree that neither the subject in any more detail than in the minutes, nor the name is mentioned by just a brief inspection of that material, would it be of any assistance to have it all translated in order to make sure that it's not -- I mean, the parties could stipulate on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I mean, the problem, of course, is that this material arrives at the last minute. The witness is placed on the list at the last moment. Our investigators are working over the weekend trying to obtain material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's -- as you know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The Defence team is placed under particularly constrained circumstances in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's also the reason why I'm trying to resolve this matter, rather than to ask the witness to read a perhaps 80-page document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But the document is there. It's available. And Your Honour's suggestion is taken on board. And it is a sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, I take it you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If we can have a copy. We'll get with the language assistant and have a look through it and decide whether it needs to be interpreted and what we can agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Mr. Davidovic, you would of course concede that it's very dangerous to rely on statements of other people in relation to matters that you have not witnessed yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What is very dangerous? I stand by what I said. Somebody may challenge it, but that's their own affair.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As a -- as a police officer, you know -- as an experienced police officer, you know the danger of relying on statements made by other people about what was said to somebody else, as opposed to you being present, witnessing or hearing something. You understand that distinction, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the difference, but I'm trying to answer the questions you asked me that are covered in my statement. If you put a specific question to me, I will answer it. I can take somebody's statement and maybe it won't check out. I'm sure if you bring Dragan Micic, he will be able to confirm this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Davidovic, our investigators have also had the opportunity to speak to Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I'll come back to that topic later. But what I want to come to now is this: Mr. Davidovic, you are a criminal. I take it you deny that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that form of the question. If there's a specific criminal offence that she says he's charged with, she should ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put it to the witness in a way that he at least understands exactly what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, what do you call a person who uses his position and police affiliations and under cover of his job transported Muslims from Bijeljina for money? What do you call that person? Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. person a criminal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it seems that you want to confront the witness with certain behaviour. Certainly that might assist the Chamber. But to put these questions in terms of whether you're a criminal or not, I mean, that's a qualification which --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm interested in his opinion as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before I proceed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please confront the witness with the fact you want to confront him with. And then if at a later stage there's any need to hear the opinion of this witness about the criminal character of the behaviour you confronted him with, then we'll see whether that would still assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you used your position and your police affiliations under cover of your job to transport Muslims from Bijeljina for money. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very heavy accusation, and these insults are very serious. I'm finding it hard to believe that this is actually happening. But let me say this: It is true that whenever I had the opportunity, whenever somebody asked me, I would help people - first of all, my friends - and accompany them to Serbia and facilitate sheltering them. It is true that whenever I was in a position to do so, I helped anyone who asked me. And I would ask you to tell me the name of a single Muslim who ever gave me any sum of money or anything that could be qualified as material assistance. Tell me the name of a single man who bought me as much as a cup of coffee for the help I gave them. And while you're at it, you might also mention what motivated me in helping those people. Calling somebody a criminal because they wanted to save another person's life is terrible. Those people had no other choice than to flee and to seek shelter elsewhere. That was their only chance. We're talking about the period when the war was only starting and people were being brutally taken away either to camps or towards the border to be killed by night. That you should call me a criminal for trying to save those people is beyond the pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, in your answer, you indicated, "I would ask you to tell me the name of a single Muslim who ever gave me any sum of money or anything that could be qualified as material assistance. Tell me the name of a single man ..." Now, I will take up that invitation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Edib Hujdurovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hujdurovic. Yes. What is it about?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Married to Jasminka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And a veterinarian?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You indicated that he was in mortal danger from Drago Vukovic and you offered your protection and promised to get him out of Bijeljina for money, which you did. Now, please give the Court your response to that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you in detail. Edib Hujdurovic is my kum. I was in Belgrade when I heard from his wife Jasminka that he had been taken away from the shop where he was working as a shop assistant. It was a veterinarian shop, selling medicine and other supplies for animals. He was taken away in broad daylight. He was brutally beaten up in the middle of the street. He was beaten so badly that he was starting to spit blood. He was taken away. Nobody knows where. When Jasminka Hujdurovic asked me - and I know her very well too. She used to be a judge in Bijeljina - I came to Bijeljina - it was a Friday - to see what it was all about. I found out that Edib was gone and that he had been taken away from his home. I went to the police to make inquiries to find out where he is. They wouldn't tell me anything. I have to tell you one thing though: When what happened happened, Jasminka came to my home and asked me to get in touch with her, and she wanted somebody from my family to accompany her, my father, mother, or son, because she was afraid for her life. She wanted to go and find Mauzer to get him to bring her husband back. My son went with her to the headquarters of Ljubisa Mauzer, and there in the headquarters, among other people, there was Commander Simic, who is now general, and some other people. When my son arrived together with Jasminka, Mauzer summoned him first. He said, "You, boy, come in." He was 17 years old at the time. Mauzer then took a portable radio and hit him on the head with it, and he said, "Why ever did you come here together with this balija woman and where is your commie father now?" When I came to Bijeljina, I found out that Edib Hujdurovic was first taken to the abandoned schoolhouse at Hase, where he spent some time, and then later that evening he was brought to the football pitch in Lopare, where he was locked in the changing rooms, or rather, in the toilet of that building. I have to mention that I was born in Lopare and I have family there. So I managed through a doctor and a man who was together with that doctor to get them to see Hujdurovic, to check his physical condition, because we knew he had been beaten and that he had been bleeding and we were afraid that that would seriously and permanently affect his health, because he had already undergone one operation and he had one kidney left. The doctor with the driver went to the football pitch and found Edib Hujdurovic lying on the tile floor in the toilet with nothing underneath. They noticed haematomas all over his body, and they reported back to me that he was in a very serious condition. That doctor even wanted it put on record by the person who was in charge of that camp. I learned about that, and I begged the doctor to find a way to transfer him to the medical centre in Bijeljina, and he was indeed transferred by an ambulance. He was admitted to the department of surgery by a Dr. Popovic, Milenko Popovic, a surgeon. And when this surgeon saw him, he said that he needed continued treatment because he already had one kidney missing and that treatment had to be administered in Belgrade. He made a medical record of that, and that is part of the official record, after which I drove Edib to Belgrade. And I have to say that I had never seen anybody who had been beaten up worse than he was. He had so many external injuries. I had never seen the like of it. I showed him first to my colleagues in my brigade and used the official car to drive him to the military medical academy in Belgrade, and I found there a doctor who had previously worked in Bijeljina, a Dr. Skataric. I asked this doctor to examine Edib, which he did. He gave him the necessary medication, and he said he had to be -- he had to lie down and to stay in a recumbent position but he could not hospitalise him at the military medical academy. So I brought him back to Bijeljina, where I found a place for him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I brought him back to my apartment in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then a request came from Bijeljina, a dispatch, saying that I had taken Edib Hujdurovic to Belgrade personally, that I had put him up in my own flat, that I was assisting Muslims. And I am not ashamed of confirming that. I am proud of that. I believe that I helped as many people as I was able to. After which, both Edib and I were taken to the SUP, the Secretariat of the Interior, to be questioned. And the main questions they asked, they kept asking, were whether he paid me or whether I profited in any way from giving him that service. Mr. Edib Hujdurovic and his wife live in Sarajevo, can confirm that not only did they not pay me any money but I gave him some money for the most basic expenses. The day I brought Hujdurovic to the military medical academy, I also took him to the International Red Cross office in Belgrade, and he was interviewed about the whole thing by somebody from the international community. I don't remember the name of the man. I wrote an official note about that to report to my superior officer all the details. Edib Hujdurovic was taken by the police to Sremska Mitrovica, where he was beaten by Sremska Mitrovica policemen at the SUP, and they kept saying, "Tell us, did you give Mico anything? Did you give him any money?" And they were trying to get him to say that he had paid me. And when he wouldn't say that, they continued beating him. The second day, which is the third day after we came to Belgrade, they returned him to Bijeljina, turned him over to the SUP, to the police, and that was when Drago Vukovic, chief of the secret police, and Predrag Jesuric, took him to his home, demanding from his father to sign away his house and his property to their friend from Tuzla, who was in fact Mauzer's uncle, in exchange for Edib's release. At 1.00 a.m. at night Edib's father signed in front of the registrar, whom they had brought by night, a document signing away his house and property, and in exchange for that Edib, his wife, and his children received passports. Mauzer put them all in his car, drove them to Belgrade -- in fact, not all the way to Belgrade but just across the border. And from then on they went by another car. After seeing them off, Mauzer gave them 100 Deutschmark as thanks. He was cautioned not to call me when he came to Serbia for the second time, but he still called me, and I brought him up to date on everything that had happened since he had been taken away from my flat. And I can state with full responsibility that everything I stated had to do with the help that I genuinely extended to help the people who needed it, to save the Muslims. And this is just an example of the things that were done to them and the objective that was pursued in doing so, and that is why I view any claim that I received money for it as extremely insolent and out of place. There are many, many Muslims in Bijeljina who wanted to save their skins and asked me to help them, and I did wherever I could. However, after this incident involving Edib Hujdurovic, the police from Bijeljina searched my house, maltreated my parents and my family, and from that time on I was under constant surveillance by the police and individual policemen, who followed my every move and every contact I had in Bijeljina, so that at the time it was very dangerous for anyone to be in touch with me, because they thought of me as a man who was spreading information beyond Bijeljina, telling people what was going on and they considered me a danger. I would now, however, like to hear from this lady on what basis she's claiming that I did what I did for money. Mr. Edib Hujdurovic and his wife had been abroad in the meantime. They are back in Sarajevo now, and they, too, can have their say. As for me, I can only be proud of the fact that I always helped people, wherever and whenever I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
