utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. So you deny that you took money in those circumstances; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely and categorically so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you also mention in your answer that you wrote an official note about that "to report to my superior officer all the details." Now, when did you write that note?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the very day that I got to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And to whom did you address the report to specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant, Spasoje Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And do you have a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I can check it out. Because afterwards, when proceedings were underway, I had the opportunity to see everything that individuals from Bijeljina wrote when they were claiming the same thing that you are claiming, and that's precisely the group that was involved in ethnic cleansing in the area of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, okay, so you didn't keep a copy of the report yourself and you don't remember who you sent the report to specifically; is that correct? The name of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the first part of your question misstates the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was Spasoje Bogdanovic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Did you address this report to anybody else or just to him? Did copies go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I addressed it to him on the first day that I came to Belgrade, and he or the federal SUP will have the relevant documents, and I have kept a copy but I don't think I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just going back to reports. You'll recall earlier today I was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. asking you about the documents that you had in Belgrade, and there was a search of your apartment in 1995, and a certificate was left for you in relation to the material that had been taken. Do you have a copy of that certificate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I submitted it to the Prosecutor. It says: "Documents taken in relation to activities in Bosnia and Herzegovina." They did not list every individual document, but I had it all in a folder and it was all there, in relation to all those events.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to your answer on that point, in response to Judge Hanoteau's question on the 9th of June at page 81 and page 82, you indicated that "They issued a certificate which showed that they had taken items that were of interest to the Davidovic case in Bosnia and Herzegovina." What did you mean when you said "the Davidovic case in Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the interest of the service in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So when you said "the Davidovic case," you were not referring to a court case. You just meant the matter of Davidovic. Is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this dossier, that folder that was taken out of my flat, was taken, and the reference was to Davidovic's activities in Bosnia. I think that was the exact wording. It is an entire folder, as I said. About 100 documents in the folder.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, just going on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question. And at the same time, Ms. Loukas, you are closer to the microphone that's off than to the one that's on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, you did talk to us in quite a lot of detail about this veterinary surgeon, and in fact I would like you to give us some explanation. Why was he found on the street in the state that you have described? In fact, why was he beaten up? What did you find out about this? What information did you gather about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that he was beaten up in the street, what happened was that he was dragged out of his shop, from the shop which was still publicly owned, as it were, at the time, at 3.00 p.m., and he was brutally beaten both within the shop and outside in the street. And it was owned by passers-by. There was a great deal of shouting and screaming. It is close to the market where it's always rather crowded, and there were women screaming. But that was only one of the cases that I referred to. I mean, I talked about Edib Hujdurovic, but it was common practice for them to pick up Muslims from their homes, from their jobs during the day and during the night. And even from their jobs, as I said, and very few of them actually had jobs at the time. And for the simple reason that they were Muslims and they had stayed in Bijeljina, and they tried to create the preconditions for other people who had come from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be housed in their houses. Hujdurovic was one of the last ones who had been taken out of Bijeljina because -- I think this was in 1994, and a huge number of Muslims had already been deported before that. About 10.000 people had been forcefully deported from Bijeljina. As to Hujdurovic, I must give you another quite interesting piece of information. The Hujdurovic family was an old bourgeois family. For hundreds of years they had lived in Bijeljina. And it's a family where everyone went to school, were well-educated, went to university. And when initially they first started with this ethnic cleansing of Muslims and chasing them away from Bijeljina, what they cared about was for respected citizens to perhaps stay. So that was a kind of showcase for anyone from the outside to see that not all the Muslims had gone; for example, that famous and well-known family Hujdurovic was still there. And since they were well-respected in town -- I'm going to give you another detail. When World War II broke out in Bijeljina and when the Ustasha and the Germans came and took the city of Bijeljina, the Ustasha wanted to demolish the Orthodox church in Bijeljina. At that point, a group of respected Muslim citizens of Bijeljina rose up and defended the interest of Serbs and they said, "Don't do it. These people are our neighbours. Don't demolish their church, because we'd rather you killed us rather than demolish the building, the church." And the Ustasha killed Hujdurovic Edib's grandfather on that occasion in 1941 for the simple reason that he opposed the destruction of the Serb church. And then in 1994, those same Serbs -- of course not all of the Serbs but certain Serb individuals engaged in such brutal behaviour at the expense of his grandson and deported him from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Now, just going back to another matter in your evidence. At page 76 of the transcript of the 10th of June, for the benefit of the Court, you gave some evidence there about -- now I'll just remind you of it. This is at page 75 and going on to page 76. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No. No. I'm quoting to you from the evidence that you gave last Friday, not from your statement, Mr. Davidovic. You stated this - and I'll read slowly so that I don't make it difficult for the interpreters - it was in relation to matters that are contained within paragraph 158 of your statement, but leaving that aside, we're actually going to the evidence that you gave on this topic. You say: "First of all, I must say that I had that conflict with Djurkovic only after I had left Bijeljina with my unit. That was one weekend when I came to Bijeljina. I cycled to town -- or rather, I went to a certain place, and when Djurkovic saw me, he stopped and he started asking me who I was, who I thought I was, why I was trying to prevent them from doing what they were doing. He said he was the only person who had the authority to do what he was doing. There was a tense situation when he said, 'Who authorised you to act in such a way?' And then he showed me this document, and it said that Djurkovic from Bijeljina had been authorised to resettle people in a humane way, and it said that they shouldn't be obstructed and it said that the president of the Assembly in the heading of the document, and there was Krajisnik's signature." Now, first of all, Mr. Davidovic, I put it to you that there was no such document as you've indicated in your evidence. Now, there's no need to repeat all your evidence again in that regard. I'm putting a matter to you, which you can either confirm or deny. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can confirm what I've said before, and I can add further details if you are interested in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, further on in your evidence, on page 76, you indicated that you spoke to Dragoljub Micic. And -- and he said: "I can't confront that. I'm familiar with that very same document," and he said that he had heard -- he said, "Mr. Krajisnik had been told about this and Krajisnik replied that he should not meddle. That's all I can say about that." Do you recall the -- the part of your evidence that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, our investigators have had an opportunity to speak to Mr. Micic about the evidence that you've given, and he indicates that -- that it's incorrect to say that he had any discussions with Mr. Krajisnik of this nature. Now, again, I'm providing you with the opportunity to reconsider your evidence in light of the fact that Mr. -- Mr. Micic has been spoken to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is that this witness has said Mr. Micic said he spoke with Krajisnik. Now, Mr. Micic is saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- he didn't. He's not saying he didn't tell Mr. Davidovic that he had spoken with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I noticed this matter. But let's -- let's -- of course, that is suggested more or less. I have not been present. Mr. Davidovic, the -- Ms. Loukas has told you that the investigators have spoken to Mr. Micic, who denies that what you told us that he told you has happened. Ms. Loukas wants to know from you whether this information changes your mind in any way as to the correctness of your testimony where you said that Mr. Micic told you that Mr. Krajisnik had been told about this and Krajisnik replied that he should not meddle. Does the information give you any reason to review your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to confirm once again I have no reason whatsoever to change anything. I stick by my previous statement. Mr. Micic told me in person that he saw that document. He said he talked to Mr. Krajisnik, and he said that Mr. Krajisnik told him not to interfere. Please, you can't even expect Mr. Dragan Micic to say anything else because he's a member of the Serb Democratic Party in parliament, and it's the same group of people doing all that. So I don't expect him to try and -- I don't know. If he is a truthful man, he will confirm it. If he doesn't want to say that, it's his right. But I'm only saying this because he said it to me himself and he said he disagreed but he could not influence this in any way and he couldn't change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm about to move on to another topic, and there's some other material that I need to check with Mr. Krajisnik, and in those circumstances I'm just wondering if we could take the next break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would, then, have a long last session because --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: A very long last session, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if we would have a break now, we would resume at quarter past 12.00 and it would take us one hour and a half for the last -- until quarter to 2.00. We'll adjourn until quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just prior to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- coming in, I might indicate that I am in the process of still receiving material and confirming material and analysing material from the investigators. Your Honour, there's no question that I would be able to complete my cross-examination. It would require this witness having to come back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When for the first time have you started enquiring into the -- well, I would say, the background and the -- of this witness, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the information that this witness was to be called, I think, came in April. Your Honours are aware that there was an application --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I was a witness, you would say this is not an answer to my question. I mean, you are now pointing at when you heard for the first time. My question was simply when did you send out the first --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Notice to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I need to confirm the precise date, Your Honour. Because I think the application was made by the Prosecution and we didn't receive the actual statement of the witness until sometime subsequent to that. And I will just confirm the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could you assist the Defence? Do you know when the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're checking to see if we can give you that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To see whether you come to the same date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate that my instructions are that the -- I think some material became forthcoming after, I think, the statement was made available by the Prosecution, but then, of course, other inquiries had to be made and inquiries continued and, of course, inquiries in relation to other witnesses are occurring simultaneously. So I think there's been a real juggling of priorities in relation to this particular witness on the part of the investigation team. And additionally, of course, the actual date when the witness was to be on the witness schedule was relatively recent in itself. And I stand to be corrected by the Prosecution as to precisely when the Defence were told that this new viva voce witness was actually going to be before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears that the statement was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disclosed at the same time we made the filing to add this witness, which was on the 7th of April. As to the first time we gave them notice of a potential date for his appearance, I can't tell you that right now because that's changed so many times I have to go back and consult e-mails and my colleagues to figure out when that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please try to find out and inform the Chamber about it, whether it will be you, Mr. Hannis, or you, Ms. Loukas. Then I've got a question before we continue with the witness, and that's of a totally different nature, although, it's related to the issue you just raised, is: Who would be the next witness? Because last week there was some -- there were some observations where the Chamber invited the parties to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 636 would be the next one. And ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I can indicate, Your Honour, that Mr. Stewart will be dealing with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And then, Ms. Loukas, since the witness is not here at this moment, you -- you -- you had a line of questioning about receiving money for transportation of Muslims. Will the Chamber hear now or in the further future more about that? Because it ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll then wait for that and -- Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, Ms. Loukas will continue her cross-examination. You may proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, I'm just going back to your statement, which I think you have before you. Now, just in relation to paragraph 11, you indicate there that there were some 25 members of the local SDS Main Board in Bijeljina, a political party which was seen as being made up of criminals, primitives, the uneducated, and menial workers. And you mention some names there, including Dr. Novakovic. Now, are you saying that Dr. Novakovic is a criminal or a primitive or an uneducated or a menial worker?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, when I read the statement when I came here to The Hague and I mentioned this to the Prosecutor, I -- what I meant was the main committee that took the initiative and set up the party. And for the most part people who were members were primitive people, simple, uneducated. But I'm not saying that Mr. -- Dr. Novakovic is an uneducated person. But he was an alcoholic, an ex-alcoholic, who had been treated on a number of occasions as such in hospital, and in the environment that he lived in he enjoyed no respect at all. If this is what you want to know. I mean, if you're asking me about this person in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you about the statement you've made in your statement. Now, how about Boro Cosovic? Are you saying that he's a criminal, a primitive, an uneducated or menial worker?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to say that he's a criminal or a primitive, but there were court proceedings there with regard to some illegal dealings, some unlawful construction that he was involved in prior to the war, and I don't know what happened in the end. But I do know that this was a matter treated in court and serious talks were held and SUP, where I worked at the time, was involved in this issue in relation to Mr. Cosovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: How doubt Zdravko Ljubinkovic? Is he a criminal or a primitive or uneducated or menial worker?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that he does not fall into the category of highly educated intellectuals. Some of his actions and some of his behaviour sometimes point out to rather primitive views, but it is a matter of personal behaviour. An inclination to drink and to do certain other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, does your perspective on the SDS party as being a party of criminals, primitives, the uneducated and menial workers, does that have anything to do with your political perspective as a communist?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't view it as a communist. Quite the contrary. I'm referring to people's characters. I'm well-acquainted with the structure of the population that set up the SDS, and I know full well what the categories and what the level of people who joined that party were. I can say it with a high degree of certainty not as a communist or a police officer, but I do know that these people never enjoyed a great deal of respect in the areas where they lived and that -- they never had a great deal of power or respect once they came to power, and we all know by what process they came to power.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Through democracy and public elections, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that full well. I know what democracy is and how public elections are meant to be operated. I must tell you, madam, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene here. It is clear that the witness keeps not in high esteem the 25 SDS people. To start any line of questioning on how power was gained, the Chamber has heard some evidence about elections. The Chamber has heard evidence about other matters as well. It really does not assist the Chamber here to start a discussion on what were the -- what brought and where and when what party in power. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I'm happy to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've also indicated in your statement in relation to Predrag Jesuric that he was a lawyer and a judge prior to the war and had engaged in criminal activities before that. What criminal activities are you talking about, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Money laundering. He was one of the leading figures involved in money laundering in Bijeljina. He even neglected his job as a lawyer and he only did that and he had people who worked for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: What's he currently doing, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean now?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean? Mr. Jesuric or myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Jesuric. What is his current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of months ago he opened a lawyer's office once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to your paragraph 13 in your statement, shall we? "After the elections, the SDS came to power and as a result I was dismissed from my job as chief of police." So I take it there that you blame the SDS from losing your job as chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not blaming SDS. Had I wanted to be a member, I would have been in. They offered me to stay, to join in, and to even be promoted. I disagreed with the political profile of that party. Any party that is called "Serbian democratic," et cetera, "Serbia," sounded like something which was not progressive. I am not in favour of nationalism, and this is not acceptable to me and I don't need to go into this anymore. And this was the reason why I didn't want to go along with it. And the difference between my own views and the views of the SDS, if I may say so, is that we are at two opposite ends of the spectrum and we have nothing in common. Had I wanted to join in, I would have done it. I was offered promotion. I was offered a place within the party, et cetera, but I turned it down. And I'm fully aware of -- and I was fully aware of what would have happened if they gained power.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, you -- you were aware, of course, that the SDA, as a Bosniak Muslim nationalist party, was actually formed prior to the SDS? You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Defence counsel kindly get closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Connotation, both parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just in relation to your paragraph 13, where you indicate that you were dismissed from your job as chief of police, that, of course, was the result of a Bosnia-wide agreement between the parties where there was a division of power in relation to each municipality, whether it was a -- a Serb-dominated municipality or a Bosniak-dominated municipality or a Croat-dominated municipality and a division of power was instituted Bosnia-wide, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And -- and I think in the circumstances in your local area the -- and that is in Bijeljina, the -- the head of police became a Serb and the commander was, in fact, a Muslim, Hasan Osmanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name exactly, but it's true. A Bosniak became commander and a Serb was chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving on to paragraph 69 in your statement. You indicate this: "A number of Serbs in Bijeljina who didn't go along or agree with the policy of SDS were killed." Now, that's quite a claim, Mr. Davidovic. Can you give the Court names of who you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you off the cuff, but this information exists and the Municipal Assembly discussed those people by name. If I could look at the documentation for the relevant period, I could see how many dead there were in that period as well as their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you can't give the Court any specific information in relation to the names of these people that you say were killed because they didn't go along with the policy of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at Bijeljina and we wrote a brief for the Municipal Assembly session which you say was the 20th and was held in Bijeljina, this brief contained the names of persons who were liquidated either by unknown perpetrators or by members of paramilitary groups. Anyway, the perpetrators were never found.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic. You indicate in paragraph 70 that "Drago Vukovic and Predrag Jesuric had lists from the SDS of wealthy Muslims in Bijeljina." Now, Mr. Davidovic, can you comment on the fact that it appears that Mr. Vukovic and Mr. Jesuric did not ever work simultaneously in Bijeljina together?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Mr. Jesuric was assistant minister or some sort of chief in charge of foreigners in Bijeljina, and Drago Vukovic was chief of the secret police. Later he was chief of the section for information -- disinformation and propaganda. I think that was the name of his position. They were in Bijeljina and they worked on different positions. Jesuric Predrag was in charge of the local police and Vukovic was chief of the secret police and later chief of propaganda. And they had a certain rating ascribed to every Muslim, and according to that rating they would be taken away. Or rounded up.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of an incident at the bridge in Sremska Raca where a group under your command took gold jewellery from Husein Kurtic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Are you aware?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who that is, and I don't know what the role of my unit is supposed to be. I had some information about seized jewellery. I know that there was a dentist - although I'm not quite sure about it - had received a large amount of jewellery, gold jewellery, from a woman and it was taken away by Drago Vukovic. That's all I know. I know that jewellery was seized from him in the amount of two kilos by this group called Yellow Wasps. That amount of jewellery was stored at the SUP. That's all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you know anything about people from your unit beating a Mr. Fadil Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know that name. Who is it? Why was he beaten?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So you know nothing of Mr. Fadil Sainovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know anything. If one of my people beat him, you'd have to give me some details.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, on to another topic. Do you know anything of Mr. Ferid Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zecevic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Did you lead him away from his house at some point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Ferid Zecevic is or used to be a schoolteacher before the war, and he also had a catering establishment. When the war began, he was arrested and taken into custody, detained. As far as I know, it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. public knowledge that a lot of money had been found on him -- or rather, he gave Arkan a lot of money, 100 or 200.000, after which he was allowed to move freely about town, and whenever asked, he said that he had cover from Arkan. Later he was taken to Batkovic camp. He was taken there and placed there by some military unit. I don't know why. And I think that he was killed there. From what I know, he never returned from Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So it was not you that led him away from his house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: How about Husein Apaka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him too. I know that he, too, was taken to Batkovic camp and I was present at the corps command when a military officer came to complain about Husein because allegedly when they ran into each other, Husein said something insulting and that military officer demanded that he be taken away immediately to Batkovic camp. He never returned either. I have to say that Apaka was my witness at my wedding, and I'm very sorry that I could not go to his home and tell him at the time that he should run away, run for his life, because if I had done so, I would have lost my head. But I know that he was taken away to Batkovic and never returned from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you did not lead him away from his house.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: How about --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. Well, there's his wife, children.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Tell me, how about Ejub Smaic if did you lead him away from his home?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ejub Smaic? Never heard -- who is that? Who is that man? Maybe you can help me remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I'm asking if you know of him. If you don't know of him, then we can leave that topic where it is.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just in relation to a particular document that I'm going to show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Ms. Loukas. We have copies, Ms. Loukas, or should it be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I think it should be placed on the ELMO, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there any English available, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is English or not, Mr. Hannis, so I --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's French. Well, this Chamber is able to read some French, but let's see if there's any -- perhaps we could see the top of the list first. There's the French text. Ms. Loukas, just for the record, would it not be wise to -- that we read what is on the top of the list or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm sure that the Bench has better facility in French than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, it should be on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it reads -- although the first word seems to be more English than French, from what I know from the French language. It's [Interpretation] "List of volunteers to go to the west. 12.03.93."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the heading also has name, sex, country, which appears to be in English. Mr. Davidovic doesn't speak English and I don't know about his French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear from Ms. Loukas on what she wants to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, were you aware of the European Community Monitoring Mission to Yugoslavia in around that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions on that topic, Your Honours. I can indicate, Your Honours, that as I've said, there are further matters that I need to look at, in terms of material that has arrived from the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What did you have in mind, Ms. Loukas? Just to -- I don't know how much time you'd need, how much -- how much questions you would -- how many questions you would still have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, what I am saying, Your Honour, is that in the light of the -- the further investigations that are continuing and the time required to analyse this material properly and put it before the Court, I cannot go any further with this witness today in cross-examination. I would suggest that he's a witness that should come back again and that, Your Honour, we can commence the evidence perhaps of the next witness so that we don't lose any court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the question, Mr. Hannis - and I invite you, Mr. Davidovic, to carefully listen to what has just been said - of course, we could move on with the next witness, but then, of course, the issue is whether we would give an opportunity for the Defence to further cross-examine this witness and whether that should be at a longer term or whether that would take, well, let's say, perhaps one more hour on -- tomorrow or Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess, Your Honour, I would -- I would like some information about this. I think this witness needed to return on the Wednesday. That was discussed when -- when we first talked about bringing him here. I don't know what else needs to be done. I don't know how much material Ms. Loukas has to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say this witness has to return on Wednesday, that means that he could leave The Hague on Wednesday and then still be back in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would ask the Court to inquire of him specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But from your information at this moment, it is -- he could not leave any later than by Wednesday. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I invited you, Mr. Davidovic, to carefully listen. Is that correct, that you could not leave The Hague any later than by Friday -- by Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have prior obligations that are already set, and I was told that I would be here on Monday and maybe Tuesday. I could not delay my departure beyond Wednesday. But are you telling me that I have to come back to continue my testimony or -- or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just inquiring into what is possible and what's not possible. Mr. Hannis, this Chamber has no updated knowledge about flights, et cetera. Hearing the last portion of the testimony on Wednesday morning and leaving on Wednesday in the afternoon, is that a practical possibility at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not up to date. The last understanding I had, Your Honour, was that those flights left at 10.30 in the morning. I don't know if there's an afternoon flight to where Mr. Davidovic would be going or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, on the basis of the information you have now, would it be possible to continue your cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's what I was just inquiring about with my case manager. The additional material will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour. I keep moving away from the microphone. And I do apologise to the transcribers for that. Yes. My understanding is that the additional material, Your Honour, that we are awaiting will take longer than overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, the question on -- on which we did not get a clear answer as to where, as I understand, you received a copy of the statement but it's not clear when you started making further inquiries, that question and that answer might become more relevant in --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- oh, sorry. I thought Your Honour was finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might become more relevant as it ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour. I can indicate that as I understand it, and my instructions are that -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, on the one hand, wants to accommodate the Defence because the Chamber is aware that cross-examining this witness is not the most simple part of Defence activities. At the same time, of course, there is some doubt as to whether the priorities have been set in such a way but -- that the situation could have been avoided. But rather than spend a lot of time on going in any further detail, the Chamber would, if it would be a solution, that the witness could leave on Wednesday in the afternoon. And I can imagine that direct flights might be very strict, but I don't know how many there are. But sometimes by finding other routes, sometimes it's possible to -- to fit a schedule into the remainder of the -- a flight schedule into the remainder of the programme. Then we would invite you, Ms. Loukas, then, to finish the cross-examination on Wednesday. That's what the Chamber very much has in mind. But it would certainly need further -- further inquiries. Mr. Davidovic, you have heard that the Defence still needs a bit more time to prepare for your further cross-examination. At the same time, the Chamber would like to finish your testimony, if possible, by next Wednesday and then to see whether you could return next Wednesday. We can't give you a final answer to it at this very moment because inquiries are still to be made. We'll keep you informed about whether we'd like to see you back tomorrow or on Wednesday through the Victims and Witnesses Section, and that also means that you're excused for this moment, and I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give. The Chamber cannot fully exclude for the possibility that you would have to return at a later stage, but the Chamber tries to do whatever it can to avoid travelling back and forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, first of all, Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Davidovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be: Ms. Loukas, since you said that the next witness would be taken by Mr. Stewart, whether we can proceed at this moment with the next witness. Mr. Stewart not being here but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can make a -- a very quick phone call, but I don't think there would be a problem with the witness proceeding, but I need to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd say that you would stay here for a while and then hear the first part of the -- of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And I just -- but obviously I need to make a phone call to confirm all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can do that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please do that. We will then adjourn for three minutes, I would say -- or five minutes. On the phone you can speak as quick as you want, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- yes, Mr. Krajisnik. You'd like to address us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something about this witness who just left, and I would appreciate it if we could go into private session for a while. I have a suggestion to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first in one word consult with Ms. Loukas because saying something about a witness is -- would easily Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. result in commenting on his testimony, which is not appropriate. Ms. Loukas, would you find one second to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to understand that I'm trying to express my own opinion here. This is a very peculiar situation. And if we need a consultation after the private session, then we can have one. I think what I have to say would assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This witness has been -- has been testifying in open court, Mr. Krajisnik. The Chamber at this moment does not see clearly why we should in relation to this witness turn into private session. But let me just consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was not up to date on what the status was with regard to Mr. Krajisnik representing himself and whether or not he was going to be allowed to ask this witness any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So we could use this time now, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, such an application could be made even without going into private session. Mr. Krajisnik, if you want to go into private session where the Chamber sees no reason and where you've given no reason apart from that it would assist the Chamber, the Chamber insists that you consult with Ms. Loukas. And this is not to say that you could not express your own position but not after having consulted Ms. Loukas, who might advise you on procedural matters related to it. So if you insist, fine; but not until after you have consulted with Ms. Loukas. And I'm not saying that Ms. Loukas should then present what your position is. You may do it yourself, but you'll first have to consult with her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say what I have to say in public session. There is no problem about that. It's not a problem for me to have this consultation either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do it in public session too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About everything this witness has said, there are written statements with regard to all of that taken by your investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're not allowed to comment or to explain what you will do in response to what this witness testified. That is out of the order. When you want to -- to produce whatever material you have, whether you do it now, whether you do it at a later stage, fine. You're not allowed, not in private session, not in open session, to comment on the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I withdraw this explanation. I suggest, however, for this witness to be called again afterwards and for all these people -- all those other people who had made statements to be invited as well. Because it could be almost a mini trial, because I think we can turn round and round in circles until the very end, and I assure you that there are statements denying everything that this witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, again, you are commenting on and you are telling us what evidence you'd like to be presented. It is for your counsel to call whatever witnesses they want to call, to present whatever evidence they want to present. They can, of course, not call witnesses when the case of the Prosecutor is presented, but of course they could already confront the witness with documents. As you may have noticed, the Chamber was willing to at least grant until Wednesday morning, if that would be practically possible to Ms. Loukas. But you are not in a position now to say what you think would be available to contradict the testimony of this witness. That's not within the Rules. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for warning me. So my proposal would be to set up a mini trial here, for the witness to go back home, and to call the witnesses that he had referred to, and within a day or two we could thus clear up the whole issue. This is a very important testimony, and that's why I've decided to come up with this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, exactly your suggestion or your proposal for a mini trial shows how important it was to consult with Ms. Loukas, who is aware of rules of procedure and sequence of presentation of evidence, when to respond, when not to respond, et cetera. Therefore, we have heard your suggestion. We will adjourn for five minutes, which allows Ms. Loukas to have a phone call with Mr. -- No, no, no, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd like to ask me something. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would in that case just like to ask you in case this witness continues to be examined, for me to be able to put questions to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have noticed, Mr. Krajisnik, that on the last few witnesses we allowed you to do so, and there's no reason to believe that we would change that experimental approach on the spot. Ms. Loukas, you will have five minutes to give a call to Mr. Stewart. Mr. Hannis, is it you who's going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- take the next ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Gaynor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor. Protective measures? It will be closed session or ... Could the registrar prepare for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll check and advise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that everyone is well prepared. And we'll continue in five minutes from now on. --- Break taken at 1.13 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just took a little bit longer with that phone call than I had anticipated, because at the same time I was getting a call from Australia from one of my sisters to tell me that my grandmother had died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber feels very sorry for you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But I'm ready to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We wish you and the rest of your family a lot of strength, because it -- especially if you're at such a distance, it's even more difficult perhaps because you can't be close by. And the Chamber is -- is with full sympathy for you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's -- it's just for my mother's sake, you know. I know it's a difficult time for her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We wish you and her all the strength she will need and you will need. Then although it's not a matter that should be dealt with in closed session, Mr. Krajisnik, but we'll deliver that decision in the open session as well, but Chamber does not follow your suggestion to have a mini trial in relation to Mr. -- to Witness Davidovic at this moment. We are in -- let me just see. We are in -- not yet in closed session, although all the curtains are down. Could we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any news about travelling schedules for next Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By "next Wednesday," do you mean the day after tomorrow, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not informed yet. I heard that possibly there was an afternoon flight at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That might help out, Ms. Loukas, of course depending on how much time you would still need. But Mr. Krajisnik wants to put some questions to the witness as well. But a flight of 1.00 means not check in not later than 12.00, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means, no traffic offences, 35, 40 minutes to get to the airport. That would leave us for the first two hours on -- perhaps there would be a possibility to perhaps have an early start; although, I usually have a meeting at 8.00 on Wednesday. But let's try it. So it's not yet a definite no. The parties should arrange stand-by, to accept and give whatever further information there is so that we could deal with the scheduling in the appropriate way. Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so we can let Witness and Victim know whether or not Mr. Davidovic should be brought back tomorrow any time as well, as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, Ms. Loukas, it also depends a bit on your information. If, for example, you would say, "I have some -- I received some material that we could deal with the last hour of tomorrow -- tomorrow's session and then we would still have perhaps the first part of the Wednesday morning's session, that might well fit in travelling arrangements. Unless you say, "No, we -- I always get all the material on Tuesday at midnight." But I take it that it comes in smaller portions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I -- what I will do is I will obviously keep the situation under review this evening and -- and tomorrow and inform the Trial Chamber as to whether I could consider I could use some time tomorrow afternoon. Because it seems to me the Wednesday afternoon is cutting it a little bit tight, if one takes into account cross-examination, re-examination, questions from the Judges, and also questions from Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps the best idea would be to -- perhaps to start -- to start tomorrow in the latter part of the morning session. We would then still have some time on Wednesday morning if need be. But perhaps start first with -- with Witness 636.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to propose that, Your Honour. It's my understanding from Mr. Gaynor that he thought his direct would be less than an hour. And I don't know how long cross would be, but it seemed to me that we would have some time to resume with Mr. Davidovic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The second half of the morning. And when you are still waiting for more information, then perhaps it comes on Tuesday in the afternoon, then, Ms. Loukas. That's what we are heading for at this moment. If there's any relevant information, the Chamber would like to hear that without any delay. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
